entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You drag your feet, as a hurt man would, and you count. Six grey cloaks around you, two with crossbows slung and four with swords. The ledger-house sits ahead at the end of the gate-top walk, and its door is barred on the inside, a thick bar, set in iron brackets, that a guard lifts from within. There are two shuttered windows on the side that faces the drop. And at the far end of the walk, twenty paces down the roof, you see a small low door with a hanging latch-string, the wash-house door Tessa told you of. It stands closed and unguarded, and you doubt anyone has remembered it.

At the threshold you plant your heels. Your voice comes flat and carrying. You will hear the Foreman's terms, but you see your sister alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

For a moment the escort tenses. Then the door opens and the Foreman's soft voice comes from inside. "Bring him in. He has earned a look."

The ledger-house is as you left it, the righted table, the lamp, the black scorch on the floor, the stove ticking in the corner. The Foreman sits behind the desk with a fresh bandage under his apron and the scorched ledger open under his hand. At the stove, on a stool, with a guard behind her and a needle in her fingers, sits Tessa. Her hands are bound again, but loosely, and a blood-flecked basin and a roll of linen lie on the stool beside her. She has been stitching a guard's arm. She looks up, and her eyes find you. She does not smile. She nods, once.

Alive. Whole.

You stall. You ask where she was kept, whether she ate, whether anyone laid a hand on her, and when the Foreman answers each question with the patience of a man who thinks he has already won, you ask him more. How long does the Tin Row's ledger keep a boy's count? Does the book carry the names of the dead? What happens to a hand that cannot work? He answers some and turns others aside, and he is as careful with his words as with his pen, but he is a clerk and clerks like to explain themselves. The stove ticks. A grey cloak by the door shifts and shifts again. Tessa's needle moves, slow, slow.

It is nearly four in the morning when he sets down the pen. "That is enough, I think," he says. "You are an interesting man, Emberhide, and you have bought your sister her stitching. The dawn bell will ring in two hours, and I want this settled before it."

He folds his hands over the brass beads. "My terms have changed again. Captain Vael has broken faith with me before his own men. I cannot have that, and neither can the mountain. You will swear your term on your father's blood, as before. And at the dawn bell, you will walk him to the gate and end his name with your own hand. Not a hobgoblin's, yours, in front of the Tally-sworn, so they see what a hand does when it is whole and obedient." He nods to a long shape in the corner, wrapped in cloth, with the red-and-tin sash trailing from one end. "Your axe, Emberhide. Dargan's. I kept it for the day you might need it."

Tessa has stopped sewing. Her eyes are on you, and the knife that was in her belt is gone. One of the grey cloaks stands behind her stool.

You have 1 hit point and your wrists in iron. The wash-house door is twenty paces beyond the wall. The dawn bell is two hours off. What does Korvash say or do?

His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. input.add_to_description: Day 21 ~3:30 AM (Korvash's nat-20 Persuasion): in the ledger-house she was allowed to be seen whole while sewing the Foreman's side. She signalled the clan sign for 'page, safe': while tending the Foreman she tore out the page bearing Gorrak's reduced-and-reinked debt line from the scorched ledger and hid it in her forearm bandage over the old scar.

entries.text: notebook: updated Tessa

You walk with your feet dragging and your eyes open, but you are tired, hurt and half-blind from the dark, and the walk gives you little. There are six cloaks in a tight knot around you, spears and swords, and no one lags behind. Cloud covers the sky. A torch gutters at the ledger-house door, and the door is oak and iron with a bar on the inside. The rest is shadow, and you take your eyes off it.

At the door you plant your heels. Two of the grey cloaks haul at your arm and you don't move. You say it flat and loud, so that it carries through the wood: you'll hear his terms, but you'll see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you speak a word.

For a breath nothing happens. Then the bar scrapes and the door swings, and the Foreman's small gentle voice says, "Bring him." He sounds almost pleased.

The room is warm. The stove ticks. The Foreman sits behind the desk with a fresh bandage over his ribs and his face drawn grey in the lamplight. In front of him lies the ledger, black at the edges, in an iron-bound chest with the lid propped open. Four more cloaks stand against the walls, and the six who brought you take their places by the door.

Tessa sits on a stool by the stove with a needle in her hand and a blood-spotted cloth in her lap. Her head is bandaged, and she is pale. She looks at you, and her amber eyes go wide and then quickly flat. She is whole. A guard stands a pace behind her, and she does not turn.

The Foreman lets you look. "She is whole," he says, "as promised, and I will say it again, so that it is in the ledger: she is whole, and she is useful. She has sewn my side twice tonight." He folds his hands on the brass beads. "Ask what you like, Emberhide. You may find that I am a patient man."

You ask. You keep on asking. How many hands in the ledger, and where does the tin go, and who buys it. How a man comes to write a number next to a child. You hold his eye and let the questions stack. Some of it he answers, thin and neat, in the voice of a man reading from a shelf. Some of it he doesn't.

Somewhere in the second quarter-hour, while the Foreman is explaining the price of tin to you, Tessa draws her needle through a stitch and lifts her bandaged forearm to bite the thread. Her left hand turns, palm down, thumb folded, and her little finger crooks. It is the clan sign for *the page is safe.* Her bandage, over the old scar, has a stiffness to it that was not there before. She tore it out while she sewed him, and nobody saw.

The sign is gone before the nearest guard looks. Tessa is back with her needle, eyes down, and her face is the face of a girl who has learned to be small. The Foreman does not notice, because he is busy telling you what a mountain costs.

It is twenty to four in the morning. Outside, the wind has risen, and somewhere far below you a single bell tolls the half-hour. Dawn is under three hours away. The Foreman is running out of patience, and his pen is out of its stand.

"Enough, I think," he says, and the beads click. "You have been thorough. Now the oath."

You have 1 hit point and ten cloaks in the room. The page is in your sister's bandage, and Gorrak and Dreg are somewhere in the dark with the dawn bell on their minds. What does Korvash do?

You let them walk you, dragging your hobbled feet and keeping your head low like a beaten animal, and you try to read the gate-top as it passes. The wind is tearing the torchlight into rags, and grit stings your eyes. You catch less than you wanted: six grey cloaks around you and the stair behind, the ledger-house door ahead with the bar on the outside, and a dark mass of roof beyond it that might be the wash-house. You can't tell more.

At the door you plant your heels, and when the sergeant's hand closes on your arm, you say it flat and loud, so that it carries through the wood. You will hear the Foreman's terms. You will see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

The door swings open. The room is as you left it, the stove ticking, the table righted, and a fresh scorch across the flags. The Foreman sits at the desk with his side freshly bandaged and the scorched ledger at his elbow, under a lid of iron. His beads are quiet. He has lost the mildness around his eyes, and a thinner thing has taken its place.

"The prisoner has a condition," he says to the sergeant, without looking up. "How very like him." He nods toward the inner door. A guard opens it.

Tessa is there. She sits on a stool in a small lamp-lit chamber with a hobgoblin's arm across her knees, a needle in her fingers and blood on her cuffs. Her ankles are bound to the stool legs. A knot the size of an egg still shows at the back of her skull. She looks at you through the door, and it is a single look: *alive*. Her thumb moves against the needle, once, clan-sign. *Hold.*

"There," says the Foreman. "Alive. Whole, if you are generous. She is the best mender this mountain has had in twenty years, and I will not waste her." The door closes. He folds his hands. "That is the courtesy. Now, I have no patience for questions tonight. You have shown me what a clever man you are, and I find that I do not enjoy it. The dawn bell will find this oath sworn or it will find your sister in a smaller room."

He lifts the paper from the blotter. The old terms are gone. The mule and the safe-conduct are struck through, and a new line stands in their place: *the mender to remain at Greyshaft for the term of the hand's service, and to be fed, and housed, and tended.* Below it is the term, the same year and a day. It is a short contract, and it has no tricks in it that you can find.

The sergeant has stepped back. Six cloaks stand at your back, and the iron on your wrists is wired shut. It is a few minutes past three in the morning, you have 1 hit point, and the pen is lying on the page.

What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You let them drag you, heels scraping, and you read the walls as you go. The stair has three turns. There are six grey cloaks, all cut from the same cloth, none of them Tally-sworn, and none of them speaks. Two crossbowmen stand on the gate-top walk under the lantern hooks. The ledger-house windows are shuttered with fresh iron bars, and the outer door's bar leans against the frame on the inside. On the roof beyond, the wash-house door that Tessa used to unlock has a new iron bar across it, bright and unpainted. Someone has learned from the last few nights.

At the door you plant your heels. In a flat voice, loud enough to carry, you say you'll hear the Foreman's terms, but you'll see Tessa whole first.

The sergeant pushes you through without answering. Inside, the room is much as you left it, with the stove lit and the table righted. On the desk is a new iron-bound chest, still smelling of oil, its lid shut. Beside it sits the Foreman, bandaged at the ribs, one sleeve scorched to the elbow, writing. The ledger is not in sight.

"She is sleeping," he says, without looking up. "Behind the curtain. The mender did good work on my side tonight, and she needs the rest." The curtain at the alcove is drawn. A bare foot protrudes beneath it, small, rust-red, still. "You will see her when you have spoken, Emberhide, and not before. That is not cruelty. That is ordering."

You press him, and he lets you. How does he know she is whole? He knows because he has men to keep her so. When will the rider turn back? The recall left the gate at midnight on a fast pony. Whether it arrives before the other rider reaches the Stones, he says, is a matter of speed, and he is fond of racing odds. What of the captain? Gorrak keeps his ledger and his number. What of the Tallies in the yard? Sleeping. What of the scorched book? He lifts one finger toward the chest, once, and does not answer.

Each question costs him a line of his gentle voice, and a few more minutes. You keep your chin up and your eyes moving, from the alcove to the chest to the bar on the door. By the time he sets down the pen and the stove has ticked its way through another half hour, he is no longer smiling.

"I have been patient with you," he says. "Three times tonight you have tried my arithmetic, and each time I have counted more kindly than I should. The bell will ring in a little under three hours, and I would like this settled before it does. Swear, or I send the rider I did not recall."

The six grey cloaks stand along the wall with their spears grounded. One crossbowman has come to the door. The curtain does not move. You are at 1 hit point in iron, and the chest and the book are within sight but out of reach.

It is a quarter past three in the morning. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 23 dusk (~5:20 PM): the freed Greyshaft column reached the Stones. Harrowmere folk with lanterns gathered there, Aunt Veshra among them, warned by Ushk's returning spears. Tally-sworn were to wait at the Stones under Korvash's word.

entries.text: notebook: updated Border Stones

"Then that's what we put to Harrowmere," you tell Gorrak. He looks at you for a long moment, and then, slowly, he nods. You will bring him to Hale Orrin and Veshra at the Stones and let him ask for honest pay in his own voice.

You stand and stretch. Tessa, already half asleep, slides over on her bedroll without a word, and you lie down beside her like a big brother. Pip is a small warm lump on her other side. The fire ticks down. Nothing stirs in the night but the sentries' boots.

Morning is cold and clear. The column rises stiff and quiet and takes the last long stretch of the road. The hills open into rolling pasture, with stone walls, frost on the grass, and the first smoke of far chimneys. The children begin to run ahead, and no one calls them back. By afternoon an old miner is weeping openly, not from sorrow.

At dusk, the three Border Stones stand ahead against a pale sky, and the road below them is lit with lanterns.

A crowd waits there. Herders in sheepskins, women with babes on their hips, men with staves, townsfolk in wool cloaks, and a line of children who came home before. Ushk stands among them, bareheaded, with his ten spears behind him. He must have run his people hard to be here. A small wiry figure in a patched shawl stands at the front, and she has your father's jaw. Aunt Veshra. Beside her is a lean, weathered drover with a crook, who can only be Hale Orrin. Pell is there too, and a small girl on his shoulders with a wool ribbon in her hair. She sees you and shrieks.

Behind you the column has stopped. Forty Tally spears are grounded and forty helms are coming off. Gorrak walks to your shoulder, bareheaded, burn bare to the lanterns. He doesn't speak. A murmur starts in the crowd when they see his face, and then it dies.

It is just past five. Your aunt takes a step toward you, and Tessa's hand finds yours.

What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 23, late afternoon: the freed column reached the Stones. Aunt Veshra, drover Hale Orrin and a crowd of Harrowmere folk were waiting, warned by Ushk's earlier return with the children. Korvash had promised the Tally-sworn would wait here, helms off, until he spoke for them.

entries.text: notebook: updated Border Stones

"Then that's what you put to Harrowmere in your own voice, Captain," you say. "Hale Orrin knows what the high road needs, and I'll bring you to him and Aunt Veshra at the Stones." Gorrak inclines his head and says nothing. It's an answer of a kind.

You stand, stretch your sore shoulders, and tell Tessa to budge up. She does, with a snort, and her back is warm against yours. Pip is wedged on her other side, and the fire ticks down to coals. Nothing stirs in the dark but the sentries. For once the night is only a night.

The second day on the road is easier. The ore road flattens out of the foothills into frost-bitten pasture, and the children begin to point at things: a crow, a wall, a thread of chimney smoke. The miners walk lighter. Around noon, Pip asks if the town has a clerk already. Tessa tells him it doesn't have an honest one.

It is nearly five in the afternoon when the three weathered Border Stones rise out of the grass ahead, long-shadowed in the low sun. You've stood here before, at dawn, with a promise and an axe taken from your hands. Today the road in front of the Stones is crowded. A hundred of Harrowmere's people are waiting, herders in wool and drovers with crooks, market-women, old men leaning on sticks. Ushk is among them, with his spears drawn up in a quiet line. At the front stands a broad, grey-braided dragonborn woman in a herder's cloak with her arms folded. Beside her a lean, weathered man leans on a drover's staff.

"That's her," Tessa says, very softly. She has stopped walking. Her hand finds yours. "Korvash. She's older."

Veshra has seen you both. Her arms come unfolded.

Behind you the column has halted, and Dreg's spears have taken their helms off. Gorrak stands a little apart with his bare face to the crowd. Brun has his eyes on the ground. Ninety-odd freed hands stare at the town they were taken from.

The Stones, the crowd, and the aunt who raised you are all in front of you. What does Korvash do?

Herders are there in sheepskins, women with babies on their hips, old men leaning on staves, and Pell in the front, thin and straight, with a small girl riding on his shoulders who must be Wren. Behind them, with a shawl round her shoulders and her arms folded tight, stands a tall dragonborn woman with greying scales. You'd know that stance anywhere. Beside her a weather-beaten drover leans on a crook and watches the Tally spears with narrow eyes. Hale Orrin, you guess.

The column halts at the Stones. Behind you forty hobgoblins stand with their helms in their hands. Gorrak has stopped at your left, bare-faced and very still.

Aunt Veshra has seen Tessa. She hasn't moved. Her mouth has begun to shake.

What does Korvash do?
